latin: Quid! Sine paenula<sup>1</sup> domo exire non dubitas!
Paenulam in sarcinis collocare neglexi<sup>2</sup>. Regiones meridianas semper tepidas esse credebam.
Erravisti! Aquilo saepe nobis aërem<sup>3</sup> frigidum affert. Propter hunc ventum hodie temperies frigida est.
Ubi paenulam emere possum?
Non desunt tabernae in hac via. Veni mecum<sup>4</sup>! Ecce taberna Olivae: ille mercator mihi amicisque meis vestes lautas pretio modico vendit.
Salve Oliva! — Salvete Domni! Quid vobis?
Fac videamus<sup>5</sup> paenulas. Ecce paenulae! Quanta<sup>6</sup> paenularum copia!
Quod est judicium tuum de istis paenulis cinereis? Quid de illa fusca?
Color hujus paenulae mihi non displicet. Eam probemus<sup>7</sup>!
Haec paenula tibi miro modo convenit.
Et cum paenula, visne alia vestimenta? Subuculam, mastrucam, bracas, pallium<sup>8</sup>? Quid de hoc petaso?
Haec paenula mihi satisfacit. Possumne eam cursuali perscriptione<sup>9</sup> solvere?
Perscriptionem implet et eam Olivae porrigit.
english: What! You dare (don’t hesitate) to leave home (to go out from home) without a coat!
I neglected to put [my] coat in the luggage. I thought (was thinking) the southern regions were (to be) always warm.
You were wrong (erred)! The North wind often brings us cold air. Because-of this wind, the temperature is cold today.
Where can I buy a coat?
There are many (Not there-is-shortage-of) shops on this street. Come with me! Here’s Oliva’s shop. That shopkeeper (merchant) sells elegant clothes to me and my friends at a moderate price.
Hello Oliva! — Hello gentlemen! What [can I do] for you?
Let us see (make we-may-see) [some] coats! — Here-are the coats! — What-a-great abundance of coats!
What do you think (is your judgment) about those grey coats? What about that darkish one over there?
The colour of this coat does not displease me. Let’s try it!
That coat suits you wonderfully (in-a-wonderful manner).
And with the coat, do want [some] other clothing? A *shirt, a *jacket, trousers, a cloak? What about this hat?
This coat satisfies me. Can I pay for it with a postal check?
He fills out the check and hands (extends) it to Oliva.

footnotes: Aër (gen. aëris), the air. Think of “aerial”.
Mecum = cum me, with me; similarly tecum, with you; secum, with him/herself/themselves; nobiscum, with us; vobiscum, with you[pl.].

Videam, videas etc.: subjunctive of video, -es, -ere, to see. Fac: imperative (irregular) of facio, -is, -ere, to make. [There are two other similar imperatives: duc, from ducere = to lead; dic, from dicere = to say.]
Quantus, -a, -um, is an adjective meaning how big, how large, how great; it agrees therefore with copia, abundance, and becomes quanta.
Probemus: subjunctive of probo, -as, -are. The verbs whose infinitive is in -are make the present subjuntive in -em, -es, -et, etc. (probem, probes, etc.). We shall discuss this again.

Mastruca, f., (gen. mastrucae) the (sheepskin) jacket. Bracae, f. pl. (gen. bracarum), the trousers: plural noun (does not have a singular). Pallium, n., (gen. pallii), the cloak (a city cloak or a cloak of a Greek cut).
Perscriptio cursualis, payment by postal check.
comments: This lesson provides us with a complete outline of the forms of the first declension. The 1st declension includes mainly feminine nouns and also some masculine nouns such as nauta, the sailor; agricola, the farmer; communista, the communist.
Note the long á which makes it possible to recognize the ablative singular from the nominative singular.

In the 1st declension, the dative and the genitive have the same form in the singular. Olivae, in phrase 13, is a dative. In the plural, the dative and the ablative are the same as each other in all declensions; they are always in -is for the first two declensions. We haven’t mentioned the vocative of this declension: its form is like that of the nominative.

Finally, the locative has, in the singular, the same form as the genitive (ROMae, MASSiLIae, etc.). In the plural, the locative does not exist: in its place, one uses the ablative: ATHeNis, in Athens; this noun being plural and having ATHeNae as the nominative.

Dictionaries indicate the genitive of nouns: it is enough today for you to remember that if it is in -ae, the word belongs to the 1st declension. Henceforth, when we introduce nouns to you, we will adopt the usual dictionary presentation. Examples:
There are no neuters (n.) in the first declension.

latin: Oliva sine mora paenulas affert.
Quod est judicium vestrum de istis bracis rubris?
Bracae rubrae homini gravi non conveniunt.
Subucula sub mastruca induitur.
Induit se mastruca super subuculam.
Illarum paenularum colores mihi placent.
Hoc vestimentum mastruca dicitur, illud autem pallium.
Graeci pallio induebantur, Romani autem toga.
Hi «gens togata», illi autem «gens palliata» vocabantur.
english: Olive brings the coats without delay.
What [do you think] (is your judgement) about those red trousers.
Red trousers are not suitable for a serious person.
A shirt is put on (worn) under a jacket.
He puts on (covers himself with) the shirt over the jacket.
[I like] the colours of those coats (please me).
This garment is called a jacket, that on-the-other-hand [is called] a cloak.
The Greeks wore (were covered with) the “pallium”, the Romans on-the-other-hand [wore] the “toga”.
The later (these) [were called] the “toga-clad (toga-ed) people”, the former (those) on-the-other-hand were called the “pallium-clad [pallium-ed] people”.
